HR@10 with one positive and 99 unique negatives measures success within a 100-item candidate set. It does not estimate full-catalog HR@10 directly: Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model orderings even in expectation. Fixed candidates improve comparability but do not remove this discrepancy. Report the benchmark explicitly as sampled-candidate HR@10; avoid claims about full-catalog ranking. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

For this benchmark, a practical uncertainty analysis is a category-stratified, paired user bootstrap: resample the 200 users within each category, retain each user’s candidates and both models’ hit indicators, calculate category mean differences, then average the four differences equally. Report the observed macro improvement and a bootstrap interval. Pairing requires identical resampled user indices across models, consistent with [SciPy’s bootstrap definition](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.bootstrap.html). This application assumes users are suitable independent sampling units; overlapping users require clustering. The interval describes user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fitted models and observed candidate sets; it excludes training-seed and candidate-redraw variability. The fixed benchmark score itself has no sampling uncertainty once predictions are fixed.

Repeatedly selecting architectures, checkpoints or hyperparameters on these same validation users creates selection optimism. Bootstrapping only the selected winner does not correct that search or provide selection-adjusted coverage. Label such intervals descriptive and conditional, disclose search extent, and reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched final evaluation after selection. Independent evaluation or nested selection is needed to assess the selection procedure itself. [Cawley and Talbot](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume11/cawley10a/cawley10a.pdf).
